steps.title: You are not supposed to hear every word
steps.html:
Read this before the recordings. You will use it immediately.

In an extended piece of speech it is very hard to hear every word, and you are not meant to. The unstressed words are spoken extremely quickly, and most of them are grammar words: articles, pronouns, auxiliary verbs, prepositions.

The stressed words are the ones that carry the meaning — usually nouns, main verbs, adjectives and numbers. Listen for those and let the rest go past.

This is why a transcript looks so much longer than what you thought you heard. In These foods were first introduced to the rest of the world during a process known as the Columbian Exchange, the words that carry it are foods, first, introduced, rest, world, process, known, Columbian Exchange. The others fill the gaps.

The practical consequence: if you miss a word, do not stop. Stopping to work out one unstressed word costs you the next stressed one, which is the one that mattered.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: The speaker says Ireland 'had become so dependent on potatoes that when the crops failed, a million people died'.
steps.prompt: What does the construction so … that do here?
options: It softens the claim, because the writer is not certain of the figures.
It presents the deaths as a consequence of the dependence, not simply as something that happened afterwards.
It compares Ireland with the other countries mentioned.
steps.answer: It presents the deaths as a consequence of the dependence, not simply as something that happened afterwards.
steps.why: So X that Y makes Y follow from X. A sentence with and then would only put them in order.

steps.title: The full clause, the reduced clause, and the participle
steps.html:
Lessons 29 and 30 side by side, because they do the same job by different means.

Both structures attach information to a noun. A relative clause keeps the pronoun and the verb: Quinoa is a grain which is grown in the Andes.

A reduced relative clause drops the pronoun and the be: Quinoa is a grain grown in the Andes. This works whenever the relative clause is passive or continuous, and only then.

A participle clause at the front of a sentence attaches to the whole clause rather than to one noun, and usually carries a reason or a time: Thinking they were dangerous, people avoided them.

Watch the direction. -ing is active — the noun does it. -ed is passive — it is done to the noun. People thinking they were dangerous = the people thought. Foods introduced in the sixteenth century = somebody introduced them.

And keep the comma rule from Lesson 29: a reduced defining clause takes no commas; a reduced non-defining one does. a grain grown in the Andes — defining. Quinoa, grown in the Andes, is rich in protein — non-defining.

steps.title: When you can reduce, and when you cannot
steps.html:
1. Start with Quinoa is a grain which is grown in the Andes. The relative clause is passive, so you can drop which is: a grain grown in the Andes.
  2. Now try Chillies are a plant which grows all over the world. This clause is active and simple, not passive or continuous. Dropping which gives a plant grows all over the world, which is not English.
  3. The rule: you can reduce a relative clause only when it contains be — that is, when it is passive (which is grown) or continuous (who are working).
  4. If you want the same density with an active simple verb, use a participle clause instead: a plant growing all over the world. It means slightly less precisely, and it is what writers do.
  5. Last check: commas. Defining → none. Non-defining → both. Quinoa, grown in the Andes, is rich in protein.

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least three reduced relative or participle clauses, and at least four adjective + preposition pairs.
steps.placeholder: It is hard to imagine … without …
steps.html:
• Open with a food and the claim that it has always been there.
  • Say where it came from, using a reduced clause.
  • Say how it was received, using a participle clause with <i>thinking</i>.
  • Close with what has happened to it since.

Useful language

  • …, a … grown in / brought over from …
  • It is hard to imagine … without …
  • Initially, people were suspicious of it, thinking …
  • … had become so dependent on … that …
  • … is now strongly associated with …
  • It is extremely rich in …
steps.modelHtml:
The vegetable nobody here can do without

It is hard to imagine our food without potatoes, and yet the whole country managed for most of its history. Brought over from the Andes, and grown here on any scale only since the nineteenth century, they arrived as a curiosity.

Initially people were suspicious of them, thinking anything that grew underground was unfit to eat. Within two generations the same households had become so dependent on them that a bad year showed up in the health records.

Today the dishes most strongly associated with this region all contain them, and nobody is aware of, or interested in, where they came from. That is the usual pattern. A food is foreign for about a hundred years and then it is not.
